verses.text: Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and a brother of James, To those who are called, loved by God the Father, and kept in Jesus Christ:
Mercy, peace, and love be multiplied to you.
Beloved, although I made every effort to write to you about the salvation we share, I felt it necessary to write and urge you to contend earnestly for the faith entrusted once for all to the saints.

For certain men have crept in among you unnoticed—ungodly ones who were designated long ago for condemnation. They turn the grace of our God into a license for immorality, and they deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ.
Although you are fully aware of this, I want to remind you that after Jesus had delivered His people out of the land of Egypt, He destroyed those who did not believe.
And the angels who did not stay within their own domain but abandoned their proper dwelling—these He has kept in eternal chains under darkness, bound for judgment on that great day.

In like manner, Sodom and Gomorrah and the cities around them, who indulged in sexual immorality and pursued strange flesh, are on display as an example of those who sustain the punishment of eternal fire.
Yet in the same way these dreamers defile their bodies, reject authority, and slander glorious beings.
But even the archangel Michael, when he disputed with the devil over the body of Moses, did not presume to bring a slanderous charge against him, but said, "The Lord rebuke you!"
These men, however, slander what they do not understand, and like irrational animals, they will be destroyed by the things they do instinctively.
Woe to them! They have traveled the path of Cain; they have rushed headlong into the error of Balaam; they have perished in Korah's rebellion.

These men are hidden reefs in your love feasts, shamelessly feasting with you but shepherding only themselves. They are clouds without water, carried along by the wind; fruitless trees in autumn, twice dead after being uprooted.
They are wild waves of the sea, foaming up their own shame; wandering stars, for whom blackest darkness has been reserved forever.
Enoch, the seventh from Adam, also prophesied about them: "Behold, the Lord is coming with myriads of His holy ones
to execute judgment on everyone, and to convict all the ungodly of every ungodly act of wickedness and every harsh word spoken against Him by ungodly sinners."
These men are discontented grumblers, following after their own lusts; their mouths spew arrogance; they flatter others for their own advantage.
But you, beloved, remember what was foretold by the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ
when they said to you, "In the last times there will be scoffers who will follow after their own ungodly desires."
These are the ones who cause divisions, who are worldly and devoid of the Spirit.
But you, beloved, by building yourselves up in your most holy faith and praying in the Holy Spirit,
keep yourselves in the love of God as you await the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ to bring you eternal life.
And indeed, have mercy on those who doubt;
save others by snatching them from the fire; and to still others show mercy tempered with fear, hating even the clothing stained by the flesh.
Now to Him who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you unblemished in His glorious presence, with great joy—
to the only God our Savior be glory, majesty, dominion, and authority through Jesus Christ our Lord before all time, and now, and for all eternity. Amen.

context.author: The letter opens, “Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and a brother of James” (verse 1). Most readers take him to be the Judas named among the brothers of Jesus in Mark 6:3, and James to be the leader of the church in Jerusalem. He does not call himself an apostle. Some scholars think the letter was written later in his name. The date is uncertain, between about AD 50 and 90.
context.genre: Short letter of warning and encouragement
context.audience: Believers who are “called, loved by God the Father, and kept in Jesus Christ” (verse 1). The letter names no town. They know the Old Testament and the Jewish books around it, which suggests a church with Jewish roots. Certain men have slipped in among them and are turning grace into an excuse for sin.
context.mapLabel: A CHURCH UNDER THREAT FROM WITHIN
context.setting: Jude had meant to write about the salvation he shares with his readers. Instead he must urge them to contend for the faith, because ungodly men have crept in who turn the grace of God into a license for immorality and deny Jesus Christ. He sets these men beside old examples of judgment, quotes a prophecy of Enoch, reminds his readers what the apostles foretold, and tells them to keep themselves in the love of God and to show mercy to those who doubt. He ends with a hymn of praise.
context.custom: The “love feasts” (verse 12) were the shared meals of the church, at which the Lord’s Supper was held. Jude uses two Jewish books that are not in the Old Testament: the Book of Enoch, quoted in verses 14-15 and echoed in verses 6 and 13, and a story about the burial of Moses in verse 9. He likes sets of three, and he ends with a doxology, a short hymn of praise of the kind used in worship.
context.timelineImmediate: Revelation follows, the last book of the New Testament.
context.timelineBible: Jude recalls Israel in the wilderness (Numbers 14), the angels of Genesis 6:1-4, Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19), Cain (Genesis 4), Balaam (Numbers 22-24; 31:16) and Korah (Numbers 16). “The Lord rebuke you!” and the stick snatched from the fire come from Zechariah 3:2-4. Verses 4-18 run alongside 2 Peter 2:1-3:3.

translation.meaning: To struggle hard, like an athlete in a contest. English “agony” comes from the same root. Used only here in the New Testament.
To keep, guard or hold. The readers are kept, angels are kept for judgment, and the readers are to keep themselves in God’s love.
To slip in by a side door. Used only here in the New Testament.
Without reverence for God. The BSB has “ungodly” six times in the letter.
Rocks under the sea that wreck ships. Some translate “blemishes,” as in 2 Peter 2:13.
Not tripping, sure-footed. Used only here in the New Testament.

overview.summary: Jude urges his readers to contend for the faith against people who turn grace into a license for sin, sets those people beside old examples of judgment, and calls the church to keep itself in God’s love and to show mercy.
overview.settingLine: From Jude, brother of James, to a church not named.

history.t: Jude is the same name as Judas. Mark 6:3 lists James, Joses, Judas and Simon as brothers of Jesus. They did not believe in him during his ministry (John 7:5), but they were with the disciples after the resurrection (Acts 1:14) and later traveled as missionaries (1 Corinthians 9:5). Hegesippus, in the 2nd century, tells of two grandsons of Jude, farmers in the land of Israel, who were questioned under the emperor Domitian and released.

The letter never names the intruders or sets out their teaching. It shows their conduct: they treat grace as permission to sin, reject authority, speak with contempt of angels, claim visions, look after themselves at the church’s meals, and divide the church (4, 8, 12, 16, 19). Later writers linked them with Gnostic groups, but nothing in the letter requires that. 2 Peter 2 describes its false teachers in much the same words, and most scholars think 2 Peter drew on Jude.

Jude was quoted by Clement of Alexandria and Tertullian about AD 200 and is in the Muratorian list. Later some doubted it. Jerome gives the reason: it quotes the Book of Enoch, which is not Scripture. Eusebius, about AD 325, placed it among the disputed books that most people knew, and the early Syriac Bible left it out. Athanasius’s Easter letter of AD 367 includes it.

customs.t: The love feast was the common meal of an early church. Believers met in a home, shared the food they brought, and broke bread together in the Lord’s Supper. Ignatius, about AD 110, and Tertullian, about AD 197, describe it, and Tertullian says the poor were fed at it. Jude’s intruders sat at these meals and looked after only themselves (12).

Jude quotes the Book of Enoch (14-15) and uses a story about the body of Moses (9) that early writers trace to a book called the Assumption of Moses. Both were known among Jews of his day. He uses them as a preacher uses stories his hearers know, and the letter does not call either book Scripture. 2 Peter, in its parallel passage, leaves both out.

Most letters end with greetings. Jude ends with a doxology: praise to the God who is able to keep his people from stumbling, with glory, majesty, dominion and authority given to him through Jesus Christ (24-25). Such lines were spoken in worship, and the letter may have been written to be read aloud to the gathered church.

archaeology.h: Jude in Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Alexandrinus
archaeology.t: Codex Sinaiticus, a Greek Bible of the 4th century, has 2 John, 3 John and Jude together on the page shown. Codex Alexandrinus, of the 5th century, ends Jude with a decorated title. The oldest copies are two papyri of the 3rd or 4th century: Papyrus 72, a small book that also holds 1 and 2 Peter, and Papyrus 78, a tiny sheet with four verses that seems to have been carried as a charm.

The book Jude quotes survives whole only in Ge‘ez, the old language of Ethiopia. Pieces of about eleven Aramaic copies were found in Cave 4 at Qumran, the oldest from the 2nd century BC, and the first 32 chapters were found in Greek in a grave at Akhmim in Egypt in 1886-87. Jude 14-15 is close to the Greek of 1 Enoch 1:9.

Mount Nebo in Jordan looks across the Jordan valley to Jericho. Deuteronomy 34 says Moses died there and that no one knows his grave. Christians built a memorial church on the summit in the 4th century. The silence of Deuteronomy about the grave is the starting point of the story in Jude 9, in which the archangel Michael disputes with the devil over the body.

overview.discussion: Jude balances contending for the faith with showing mercy to doubters. How do I hold firm and still show kindness to someone with doubts?
